prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate economic shocks, creating the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore's 'Credit Cycles' (1997) isolates a single, clearly stated mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to the value of collateral create a feedback loop between asset prices and credit. Small or temporary shocks therefore become large and persistent, and the effects spill across sectors. The mechanism is the base of a large body of quantitative macro, financial-crisis analysis and macroprudential thinking, and the 2007-09 crisis made its relevance concrete. Attribution is the cleanest of the macro candidates: one paper is the origin, and its two authors are unambiguously its originators. The contribution is also distinct from the 2022 prize. That prize rewarded bank runs, intermediation and the empirical history of banking crises. This is a dynamic general-equilibrium propagation mechanism. The work is nearly three decades old and has been extended and tested in many settings, so there is no maturity concern.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial redundancy with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and the lineage through the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator, which a sceptical member could read as the same theme. The contribution is mainly theoretical, and the size of the amplification it implies is hard to identify directly. B027 has a broader empirical base and shaped policy debates across several fields. If the Committee judges the 2022 overlap to be decisive, B006 is not the right choice this year.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B006 fourth and would add Gertler for the financial-accelerator line. He also notes that Bernanke's accelerator work was recognised in 2022 and that Gertler appears in B018.
responses.response: I agree on the 2022 overlap, but it argues for keeping Gertler out, not for adding him. The accelerator is a related but distinct mechanism, and part of its lineage was recognised in 2022. Adding Gertler would blur the citation and make part of it redundant. His wider contributions are better weighed under B018. I do not think Krusell's case for a third name is strong enough to change the configuration. We also share an institutional tie, which I disclose below.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B027 first and values its combination of clear identification and a coherent task framework. He also notes that the task and trade-shock strands might be seen as two separate prizes, and that any three-name set omits someone.
responses.response: I agree that B027 is scientifically very strong, and I ranked it third. His own concern is what holds me back. The task and skill-demand strand (Autor, Katz) and the trade-shock strand (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) rest on different identification and different credit. The Acemoglu and Goldin prizes also overlap with the field. A single citation therefore needs care, and the three-name cap forces a choice between Katz and Dorn that I cannot resolve on the evidence in front of us. B006 has no comparable split. I keep B027 as my first alternative and would accept it if the Committee finds a coherent citation.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 first. He argues that Mian and Sufi's household-debt channel was not covered by the 2022 prize, that their results have been replicated across countries, and that the timing is ripe.
responses.response: The point that the household-debt channel is distinct from the 2022 prize is fair, and it is the best answer to the redundancy worry. I still place B001 below B006. Its core results date from roughly 2009 to 2015, so they are younger. The split between credit-supply and other explanations of the housing boom is still debated, and I think the long-run verdict is less settled. B006 rests on a mechanism that has been extended and applied for much longer. I have not included B001 among my alternatives, but I regard it as a serious macro-finance candidate for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads Kiyotaki-Moore as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize and the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator lineage.
Whether Gertler, and possibly Gilchrist, should be added, and how that would interact with Gertler's appearance in B018.
Whether B027 can be given a single coherent citation across its task, skill-demand and trade-shock strands within the three-name limit.
How much weight the Committee gives to a mostly theoretical contribution with indirect empirical validation compared with strongly empirical candidates.
My assessments rely on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied opening files, and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited names of B006 or B027 is apparent from my profile. I disclose these other connections: I have co-authored with committee members Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg and frequently with Per Krusell, the secretary. Krusell and Boppart are also IIES colleagues. I am a macroeconomist, which may bias my view of macro candidates. I flagged a research affinity for dynamic political economy and social mobility in my opening, but neither candidate is part of my preferred configuration. I disclose these connections without adjudicating them.
